stories.title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia sparks bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill
stories.summary: Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is drawing criticism and scrutiny — including about national security risks — from members of Congress in both parties. Why it matters: President Trump's push to reinstate Huang creates a headache for Republicans and new fodder for Democrats eager to deploy their investigative powers when they take control in January. sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Six key questions raised by Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
sources.text: Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher. The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results . A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers. The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025. Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue. Still, the board's reversal, President Donald Trump's administration's role and continued scrutiny of Nvidia's China business leave major questions for both investors and lawmakers. Sen. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case. Reed did not lay out a specific list of questions for the two officials, but his statement cited reporting that Trump had been briefed by intelligence officials led by then-National Security Adviser Marco Rubio before intervening in support of Huang's return. Reed's call adds to mounting pressure on both Nvidia and the Trump administration to explain what they knew and when. Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., vice ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang’s reinstatement could broaden congressional scrutiny rather than bring it to a close. “I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query,” Amo told CNBC, adding that lawmakers should also examine administration officials involved in decisions affecting Nvidia and chip sales to China. Amo said he expects the planned closed-door interview with Huang on Dec. 1 to proceed and that Congress would continue seeking answers both privately and publicly in the coming months. “He should start purchasing his plane tickets to Washington,” he said. “It is abundantly clear that this is ripe for questioning by Congress.” On Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones said the board had accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Less than a week later, the board reversed course, saying Monday that it had unanimously voted to bring Huang back after discussions with him and input from senior U.S. government officials. Trump said he had spoken with board members and that his administration provided assurances based on the information available to it. But the board has not publicly detailed what it was told. "The board decided to do what we wanted to do," Trump told CNBC , adding that he believed his intervention had been important. "I've been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it," he said. Trump also called into an Nvidia board meeting to argue for Huang's return, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Reed has called on Huang to disclose his communications with Trump and on Nvidia to release a transcript of the board's call with the president. Lawmakers are still seeking answers about the alleged smuggling of Nvidia products to China, their possible diversion for military use and possible advancement of Chinese AI capabilities. The Senate Banking Committee has scheduled Huang to testify on U.S. export controls on Dec. 3. House lawmakers have also confirmed closed-door interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. "The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," Reps. John Moolenaar, Rick Crawford and Brian Mast said in a joint statement. Their inquiry may also examine what Nvidia knew about the customers and resellers involved, as well as what controls the company had in place. Other lawmakers have also sought to preserve the paper trail. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons had asked senior administration officials on Nov. 11 to retain records related to Nvidia exports of advanced AI chips to China and associated national security concerns. Nvidia has promised to hire a chief compliance officer and establish a committee overseeing national security and export controls. The board's investigation into Huang's conduct also remains underway. Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for APAC and the Middle East, said investors will be watching whether those new safeguards carry meaningful authority. Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia has a limited window to prepare for the possibility that a future president may be less supportive of Huang. With Trump's term ending in two years, Luria argued that Nvidia needs a clearer plan for who could take over if Huang were forced to leave again. Gilbert pointed to Nvidia's roughly 75% revenue-growth forecast for the next financial year as evidence of strong near-term demand. The longer-term question, he said, is whether customer orders and artificial intelligence investment can sustain that pace. Luria told CNBC that concerns about the broader AI trade remain, including the cost of financing data centers, potential overbuilding by neocloud companies and obstacles to building new facilities. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said worries about whether AI spending is achievable and sustainable were not caused solely by Huang's departure. UBS, meanwhile, flagged Nvidia's roughly $390 billion in supply commitments and the need to keep demand flowing through its ecosystem. Gilbert said part of Monday's rally reflected investors recovering earlier losses rather than pricing in new growth. Bernstein restored its "Outperform" rati

sources.title: What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia’s Colette Kress
sources.text: Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress led the company for 11 days during Jensen Huang's sudden but brief departure. When Nvidia's board officially reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, the company also announced that Kress would continue in her role as CFO. The 59-year-old Kress currently has roughly 4.775 million shares directly and indirectly held, which makes her worth approximately $778 million at Monday's market close. The 63-year-old Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia stock soared 31% and the Nasdaq surged more than 6% Monday after the company announced that Huang would return as CEO, president and board director, effective immediately. Huang returned to the office Monday to crowds of Nvidia employees cheering his return . Kress, who stepped in as interim CEO during Nvidia's moment of crisis, joined the chipmaker as finance chief in September 2013 following stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. As CFO, Kress oversees the balance sheet of a company aggressively financing many of the infrastructure deals that power the artificial intelligence buildout. Those agreements also raise concerns over circular financing and Nvidia's AI exposure in the event of a slowdown. In the first earnings call after Huang's resignation, Kress sought to reassure investors, raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue-growth forecast to roughly 75% from 70%. She told analysts during a Q&A portion that it was "business as usual" at the company. She later told CNBC's Jim Cramer that customers have stood by the chipmaker and that demand continues increasing. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do," Kress said. During the company's first all-hands meeting after Huang's resignation, Kress also struck an optimistic tone , telling employees to "move forward" and mentioning pay raises. But Kress didn't manage to impress many market participants and insiders, who compared the interim chief to Huang. Last week, the stock recorded its worst week and longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis as AI stocks plummeted. "She just wasn't him," The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman told CNBC. "I think she would have had to strengthen her bench around her a lot, because you have a visionary, product technology driven CEO that was literally the epicenter of the company. He was the entire identity." One person CNBC spoke with said Kress handled the situation with "skill and grace" while managing a tough job. The former Nvidia employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private, said Kress helped reassure the industry and that people should not be so "quick to rush to judgment." In the week since Huang's exit, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang belittled Kress, calling her "a deer in the headlights." Huang said in the press release announcing his return that he was "grateful" for Kress "leading NVIDIA during this period." "I think she is a fantastic CFO. I think Jensen probably has great confidence in her. I hope she stays," the former Nvidia employee said. "I don't think that she's going to be on thin ice when Jensen returns." Nvidia did not immediately respond to comment for this story.

sources.title: Tech sell-off resumes as euphoria from Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return subsides
sources.text: Sell-off signals investors are bracing for further volatility in key AI sector driving economic growth worldwide Technology shares led a market retreat Tuesday as caution returned after Jensen Huang’s extraordinary return to Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide. A day after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO drove Nvidia shares up more than 30%, adding more than $900bn to the firm’s market value, the euphoria dissipated as its stock lost almost 9% mid-session. Anthropic also slumped, giving up about 12% to $77.19, below its $83 price for last week’s IPO. Monday aside, AI stocks had already sold off sharply throughout November on worries about profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector. By noon in New York, the tech-heavy Nasdaq had shed 2.3% and the broader-based S&P 500 lost 1.1%, while the Dow was just into the green. Europe’s main stock markets, which feature far fewer tech companies than their Asian and US rivals, finished a handful of percentage points lower after jumping Monday in line with Wall Street. Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago over extramarital affairs, reportedly with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a senior Nvidia executive before Donald Trump noisily declared he should be brought back. “Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Charu Chanana, an investment strategist at Saxo Markets. “He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate,” she said. But “Jensen Huang alone cannot support the AI trade in the long term,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. “Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session,” she added. Analysts were in broad agreement that Huang’s return did not mean an end to investigations or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for six months. The company remains under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.

sources.title: Trump endorses Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, says US has no evidence of wrongdoing
sources.text: President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk. In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case. There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.” Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions. Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: Claude AI can review pull requests and ship fixes on its own now
sources.text: Anthropic is bringing new AI tools to software engineers with Claude Ship. Anthropic is bringing new AI tools to software engineers with Claude Ship. Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests. Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October . What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today. PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says. Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

sources.name: ZDNet AI
sources.title: Claude can ship code for you now – how to try it (if you dare)
sources.text: Would you let a few Claude agents review and ship your code for you? Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI-powered coding tools like OpenAI’s Codex in droves, but some still want to check code themselves before pushing it. A new feature from Anthropic is banking on more adventurous, agent-first coders being comfortable with handing even that last step off to AI. With Claude Ship, announced in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said. The feature is geared toward individual developers or companies who want to move faster or already delegate a significant amount of coding tasks to agents. Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code “Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person,” Anthropic said. “The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.” The new feature uses two new agents alongside Code Review , which Anthropic released in March for Teams and Enterprise plans. Code Review first collects, organizes, and posts findings to a PR. Then, Anthropic said, the agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, guide a PR “through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually.” PR Steward can’t approve or merge pull requests, designed instead to participate “on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members.” It also documents what it changed in each push through comments and provides instructions for how to undo it, should developers want to. Throughout the process, developers can give Claude instructions or tell it to stop by commenting @claude. Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free – how it went As a final step, Claude Approvals references whatever policy the user or team abides by (which developers provide as a repo file), and additional signals developers set, like Code Review findings, before approving changes autonomously if allowed. If not, it will seek out “deeper human sign-off,” Anthropic said. “It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file,” the release added. Anthropic said it recommends that most customers enable those additional checks “first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals’ green light.” Admins can select which repos the feature runs in and adjust settings as needed. But Claude Ship isn’t meant for everyone. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in the release, noting that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs. ZDNET senior contributing editor David Gewirtz said the idea of shipping code at the speed of writing it “raises the hair on the back of my neck.” But he added that, given how impressive Claude Code has been thus far, he wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic’s deployment tools were equally effective. Also: Claude Code vs. Codex: Why I use both and how to choose one (if you must) “But, it does depend on the team’s workflow and the kind of development they’re doing,” he said. “It’s not something for every team and certainly not for every indy developer, but for certain deployment processes, it could shave a ton of time off turnaround, saving money and potentially sending fixes to customers much faster. ‘Tis cool.” Ultimately, Gewirtz said he has reasons to both trust the tool and be concerned about what it means for younger developers in the workplace. “Since that workflow is often assigned to less experienced members of the team, it’s likely that Claude would be as accurate, although it’s one more way to shut the junior members out of where they add value to the company and grow their skills to become senior decision makers,” he said. Developer platforms overall are adapting to the new state of the industry. Entire , a GitHub competitor started by the Microsoft-owned platform’s former CEO, is built around the expectation that developers are working side-by-side with agents. Individuals with a Pro, Max, or Ultra subscription can use the /ship command now available in Claude Code, meaning “users won’t notice any significant increase in token usage,” an Anthropic representative explained. Team and Enterprise users can use Claude Ship for Github repos, and it is billed on tokens, so your overall bill may change. Still, that depends on the number of PRs users are putting through Claude Ship — to avoid any surprises, admins can set spending limits for both Code Review and the new PR Steward agent. They can also turn Claude Ship on for an entire repo, meaning developers won’t need the /ship command. Anthropic added that certain Enterprise organizations “can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming” by Jan. 15, 2027. Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard As with other Claude features, like the still-to-come Meetings , customers with a zero-data-retention policy and other privacy configurations don’t have access to Claude Ship. sources.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
sources.text: Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge. The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available , and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed. Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process. Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision. Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta. sources.title: Good news for AI coders — Anthropic's Claude Ship is now able to review pull requests and even ship code fixes all on its own
sources.text: Claude Ship wants to do more than generate your code Anthropic has lifted the wraps off Claude Ship in response to growing concerns that AI isn't actually helping speed up coding, but rather just pushes the bottlenecks further down the line. With its new suite of AI agents, Claude Ship will be able to automate some of the later stages of software development, like reviewing code changes, resolving problems and approving certain merges and changes, making the platform far more useful than just a code generator. The company even shared in its announcement that Claude already writes "most" of the code produced by its own Claude Code team, so it understands the ongoing constraints that developers face. Rather than being an individual agent or tool, Claude Ship is more of a suite that's made up of three distinct elements. Code Review, the first of the three, is already in place, and handles cross-checking for potential problems at three levels of detail – Quick, Standard and Deep. "On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%," Anthropic shared in a bid to quantify the tool's value. PR Steward "jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback" generated by both Claude Review and human developers, but for now, it remains in beta. And finally, Claude Approvals is responsible for evaluating some of the more routine changes against an organization's policies, routing just the most sensitive changes to human specialists. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The tools still aren't perfect, and Anthropic acknowledges that Ship can still overlook bugs, vulnerabilities and other issues – hence recommending that users enable Claude Approvals in observe-only mode at the start to build trust – but it's undoubtedly the start of something big. Coding was one of the first use cases where AI was able to offer significant productivity boosts, but it didn't take long to work out that generating faster code alone wasn't enough to speed up the entire software development lifecycle. This new phase, where AI is helping at later stages of the process, looks like it could finally deliver on those productivity promises. stories.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
stories.summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
sources.text: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements. The Shirudo technical walkthrough ⁠ (opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer. Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained. We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised. OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo ⁠ (opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL. Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches. Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart ⁠ (opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection. Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub ⁠ (opens in a new window) , read the docs ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and let us know what you find ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

sources.title: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks
sources.text: Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence . Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution. They’ve just announced a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched. In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough. According to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.” To counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so users can quickly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from previously unknown vectors. Graf said the key to doing this is to secure workloads at runtime, which is why the initial focus of Cisco’s and OpenAI’s initiative is Shirudo , an evolution of the open-source Tetragon runtime security project that aims to provide autonomous defense for AI agents. Shirudo, named after the Japanese word for “shield,” is based on extended Berkeley Packet Filter or eBPF, which is a Linux kernel technology that acts like a kind of sandbox within the operating system. Similar to how JavaScript makes web browsers programmable without a restart, eBPF enables small, verified programs to run inside the Linux kernel to observe an application’s activity and modify its behavior without altering its source code or rebooting it. Graf explained that Cisco and OpenAI chose to use eBPF because there are no other real alternatives. Human-focused security consoles and policy languages are simply too slow for AI agents, and will limit their productivity. By exposing programmable kernel interfaces, eBPF enables AI agents to capture granular telemetry, evaluate mitigations in monitoring mode and deploy cryptographically-signed shields in milliseconds. So cyberattacks that exploit unknown vulnerabilities can be blocked in real time without causing disruption to their live workloads. “There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing,” said Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out.” OpenAI’s role in this is to prove that eBPF is up to the job, and it has already deployed Shirudo as part of an agentic control plane that’s powered by its Codex coding agent. When given details of a new vulnerability, Codex can use Shirudo to autonomously build an exploit reproducer and then design a mitigation strategy. It then validates the mitigation code and deploys the cryptographically-signed shields across all affected nodes. The two partners recently tested Shirudo against a critical new vulnerability in OpenJDK called Java4Shell, and it was able to rapidly generate Java bytecode that it injected directly into a running Elasticsearch agent to block malicious Base64 overwrites that would have compromised the system. OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman said the goal of Shirudo is to help companies protect their systems from new threats until they can build and deploy a more durable patch. “When one team finds a better way to protect a system, others shouldn’t have to start from scratch,” he explained. To that end, Cisco and OpenAI say they’re welcoming developers, kernel engineers, platform builders and security experts to collaborate on Shirudo and other initiatives within their broader Secure Infrastructure Project. sources.title: OpenAI y Cisco lanzan Shirudo, una herramienta para Linux con IA que permite bloquear exploits antes de aplicar los parches de seguridad
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. OpenAI y Cisco han dado a conocer un entorno de ejecución de código abierto que protege los sistemas Linux mientras implementan parches sin necesidad de reiniciar los equipos. OpenAI y Cisco han lanzado Shirudo, un entorno de ejecución de código abierto que ayuda a los operadores a proteger los equipos con sistema operativo Linux en funcionamiento sin necesidad de esperar a que se aplique un parche de seguridad o a reiniciar el sistema. Se trata de una plataforma diseñada para ayudar a los equipos de seguridad a gestionar los procesos de desarrollo e implementación de correcciones de errores y cuyo nombre significa escudo en en japonés. La compañía de inteligencia artificial dirigida por Sam Altman ha compartido un documento en el que señala que, para crear esta plataforma, ha contado con la participación de desarrolladores, investigadores de seguridad y operadores de infraestructura de todo el sector. Todos ellos son conocedores del proceso de prueba e implementación de parches, que puede llevar días o semanas; un procedimiento que puede complicarse, cuando una vulnerabilidad y una solicitud legítima pueden depender del propio sistema. Bloquear una operación, por tanto, podría dejar offline el servicio. Shirudo, que significa escudo en japonés , está planteado para ayudar a los equipos de seguridad a gestionar esta disyuntiva y con ella, los equipos pueden probar si una medida de seguridad temporal bloquea el comportamiento que expone una vulnerabilidad, a la vez que permite el paso de las solicitudes legítimas. "Una vez que un operador aprueba el escudo, este se puede implementar sin que el servicio deje de funcionar", ha explicado la empresa en este escrito, en el que también ha detallado cómo funciona Shirudo. Shirudo es un servicio que emplea Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), una tecnología de kernel de Linux que permite ejecutar pequeños programas aislados y seguros dentro del núcleo del sistema sin modificar su código fuente ni cargar módulos tradicionales. Gracias a esto, es posible observar las actividades sospechosas y aplicar medidas de seguridad específicas a los sistemas en ejecución. Teniendo esto en cuenta, conviene señalar que OpenAI y Cisco han Shirudo en torno a cuatro capacidades principales. La primera, protección en tiempo real, debido a que estos escudos eBPF pueden bloquear rutas de código vulnerables sin reiniciar el sistema. De este modo, los equipos de seguridad pueden supervisar cómo afectaría un escudo propuesto a las aplicaciones antes de implementarlo. Otro detalle importante es que Shirudo puede otorgar controles programables a los agentes, que les permitan investigar vulnerabilidades y también desarrollar protecciones específicas frente a exploits y cargas de trabajo reales. También es importante señalar que los escudos se firman criptográficamente y se verifican antes de su carga, mientras que los controles de seguridad del núcleo kernel restringen cambios no autorizados por el programador. Finalmente, OpenAI ha dicho que Shirudo emplea lo que se conoce como Módulo de plataforma segura (TPM), gracias a lo cual generan un registro verificable de los escudos que se cargan o eliminan. La desarrolladora de herramientas de inteligencia artificial ha señalado que su objetivo a largo plazo con esta plataforma es "permitir que los defensores y los agentes de IA identifiquen rápidamente los sistemas afectados e implementen estos escudos. Sobre esto, han adelantado que se encargarán de combinar "la IA de vanguardia con la investigación en seguridad e infraestructura", a fin de descubrir vulnerabilidades y probar defensas contra ataques y situaciones reales. Shirudo se está desarrollando de manera abierta con todas las personas que contribuyen al sistema operativo Linux (concretamente, a quienes "construyen, ejecutan y protegen" estos equipos , y próximamente estará en manos de todas las personas interesadas en probarlo.

sources.title: OpenAI and Cisco team up to stop AI-generated security threats before they get too big
sources.text: Shirudo is a new AI-powered open source runtime OpenAI and Cisco want to make n-day vulnerabilities on Linux a thing of the past with Shirudo (Japanese for ‘shield’) a new tool which is being open sourced so the wider cybersecurity community can inspect it and contribute if they want. Security vulnerabilities generally fall into two broad categories: zero-day flaws, and n-day flaws. Zero-days are flaws unknown to the vendor and as such have no official patch or fix. They’re called “zero-day” because the vendors have had zero days to fix the issue before threat actors started exploiting it. Following the same logic, n-day flaws are those that are known to the vendor but have not yet been patched. This puts software users in a tricky position: do they turn off vulnerable services to protect the wider infrastructure (and thus hurt their bottom line and their reputation), or do they keep the services running in anticipation of a patch, and risk being exposed and exploited? It is this security limbo that Cisco and OpenAI are trying to solve. “Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks,” OpenAI said in an announcement . “Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.” Shirudo, which is powered by AI apparently does just that - protects Linux systems while IT teams roll out patches. Teams can set up a temporary safeguard (called shield), and test to see if it blocks behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while allowing legitimate requests through. After approval, the shield gets deployed and the service can continue unabated. OpenAI said Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system . That way, users can monitor for suspicious activity and apply targeted protections to otherwise running systems. eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, and security teams can monitor how a proposed shield affects applications before even enforcing it. OpenAI also said Shirudo was designed to give AI agents “programmable controls” to investigate vulnerabilities, build targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads, while security teams get to control what gets deployed. All shields are cryptographically signed and verified through Linux’s eBPF verifier, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Finally, OpenAI said the verification is backed by hardware: “Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.” The two companies shared a technical walkthrough from the Linux Plumbers Conference, showing how to apply the shield and verify it on the target host. They also demonstrated how Shirudo helped protect a running Elasticsearch application against the Java4Shell vulnerability by adding an input check to Java's Base64 decoder, blocking malicious input without interrupting the service. “Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable,” OpenAI and Cisco said in the announcement post. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.” Shirudo is an open-source tool, allowing developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators to inspect the code, test it, and contribute at will. It is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.
